A thermostat is a device that automatically controls temperature. Its entire purpose is one job: keep the temperature at the level you want — without you having to watch it or adjust it constantly.
What problem does it solve?

Imagine you want your room to stay at 22°C. Without a thermostat, you'd have to:

  • Manually switch on the heater when it gets too cold.
  • Manually switch it off when it gets too warm.
  • Repeat this, forever.

A thermostat does all of that for you, automatically, all day and night.
How it works — the simple version

Every thermostat works on the same basic logic:

  1. You set a target temperature (called the set point). Let's say 22°C.
  2. The thermostat has a built-in sensor that constantly reads the actual temperature.
  3. It compares the two:
    • Room feels cold (say, 20°C) → thermostat switches the heater ON.
    • Room reaches 22°C → thermostat switches the heater OFF.
    • Room drifts cold again → heater switches ON again.

This cycle repeats automatically. The thermostat is essentially an automatic on/off switch for your heating or cooling system, guided by temperature.
The small but important detail: the "dead band"

A well-designed thermostat does not switch on and off at the exact set point. Instead, it has a tiny tolerance range — say, ±0.5°C around your target. So if you set 22°C, it might:

  • Switch the heater ON when temperature drops to 21.5°C
  • Switch it OFF when temperature reaches 22.5°C

This tolerance range is called the dead band (or hysteresis band). Without it, the heater would switch on and off hundreds of times per hour, which would waste energy, make noise, and wear out the system quickly.
Where you find thermostats

Thermostats are everywhere — anywhere temperature needs to be held steady:

  • Homes and offices — control air conditioning and central heating
  • Refrigerators and freezers — keep food at a safe cold temperature
  • Ovens and microwaves — maintain a set cooking temperature
  • Water heaters — keep water at your desired temperature without boiling it over
  • Car engines — regulate coolant temperature so the engine doesn't overheat
  • Incubators (for premature babies or eggs) — maintain a critical warmth
  • Fish tanks (aquariums) — keep water at the right temperature for the fish
  • Industrial machines and labs — maintain precise conditions for manufacturing or experiments
Types of thermostats

1. Mechanical (bimetallic) thermostat
The oldest and simplest type. It uses a strip made of two different metals bonded together. Because the two metals expand and contract at different rates when heated or cooled, the strip bends. This bending physically connects or disconnects an electrical circuit — turning the system on or off. No electronics needed; it's pure physics.

2. Electronic/digital thermostat
Uses an electronic sensor (usually a component called a thermistor or thermocouple) instead of a metal strip. Far more accurate and precise. Displays the temperature on a digital screen. Found in modern homes and appliances.

3. Programmable thermostat
A digital thermostat with a built-in timer. You can tell it: "Be 18°C at night, 22°C in the morning, 18°C when we're at work, 22°C when we come home." It follows this schedule automatically every day, saving energy when no one is around.

4. Smart thermostat
The modern evolution. Connects to your Wi-Fi, so you can control it from your smartphone — even from miles away. Some models learn your habits over time and adjust automatically. They can also show you how much energy you're using.
The key characteristic: self-regulation

What makes a thermostat special — and what the word truly captures — is self-regulation. It doesn't just respond to a command once; it continuously monitors the situation and makes corrections on its own to maintain a desired state. Engineers call this a closed-loop control system or negative feedback loop:

  • A change happens (temperature drops).
  • The thermostat detects it.
  • It takes the opposite action (turns on heat) to push conditions back to normal.
  • It keeps doing this in a loop, indefinitely.

This idea of "sense → compare → correct → repeat" is the fundamental logic behind a thermostat.
The word used more broadly

Because of this self-regulating quality, the word thermostat is sometimes used as a metaphor in other fields — biology, economics, psychology — to describe any system that automatically keeps something at a stable level. For example, scientists describe the human body as having a built-in "biological thermostat" (the hypothalamus in your brain) that keeps your body temperature at around 37°C, automatically triggering sweating when you're hot and shivering when you're cold.
In a sentence
The thermostat in the living room was set to 24°C, so the air conditioner switched on whenever the room got warmer than that and turned off once it cooled down.
Summary in one sentence
A thermostat is a self-regulating device that monitors temperature and automatically switches a heating or cooling system on or off to keep the temperature at a level you have chosen.
